nib types pointed broad edge crow quill bowl poster mapping drawing
a: Calligraphy nibs fall into two main categories: pointed nibs (used for Copperplate, Spencerian, and modern calligraphy, with flexible tines that spread under pressure to create thick-thin line variation) and broad edge nibs (used for Uncial, Blackletter, Italic, and Gothic scripts, with a flat chisel tip that produces consistent thick and thin strokes at a fixed pen angle). Specialty nibs include crow quill nibs (extremely fine, rigid points for delicate detail work and mapping), bowl and poster nibs (very broad tips for large lettering and signage), and music nibs (three-tined nibs that draw multiple parallel lines simultaneously for musical staff notation). Nib flexibility ranges from rigid (extra-fine, fine) through semi-flex and full flex to super-flex (also called wet noodles), with the level of flex determining how dramatically the line width changes with pressure.

a: Pen holders for dip pens come in two primary styles: straight pen holders (where the nib aligns directly with the shaft, suitable for broad-edge scripts like Blackletter and Italic) and oblique pen holders (where the nib is offset at an angle via a brass flange, allowing the writer to maintain the proper 52-55 degree slant for Copperplate and Spencerian without twisting the wrist). Fountain pens offer convenience with built-in ink reservoirs and filling systems including cartridges (pre-filled plastic cartridges), converters (reusable piston mechanisms that accept bottled ink), and integrated filling systems like pistons (Pelikan, TWSBI), vacuums (Pilot Custom 823), and eyedroppers (where the entire barrel serves as an ink reservoir). Nib materials in fountain pens include steel (firm, affordable) and gold (springier, more flexible, corrosion-resistant), with flex nibs allowing line variation while firm nibs provide consistent marks for everyday writing.

a: Brush pens combine the convenience of a pen with the expressive potential of a brush, with popular models including the Tombow Fudenosuke (available in hard and soft tip versions, ideal for fine to medium brush lettering), Tombow Dual Brush Pens (a broad flexible tip on one end and a fine bullet tip on the other, available in hundreds of colors), and Pentel Aquash (a waterbrush with a barrel that fills with water for watercolor effects or with ink for portable brush lettering). Traditional paintbrushes used for calligraphy include pointed brushes (for fine details and pointed pen-style lettering in large formats), flat brushes (for broad-edge effects), and round brushes (for versatile stroke widths), with sable and kolinsky hair brushes offering superior snap and ink retention compared to synthetic alternatives. Japanese brush pen brands like Kuretake and Zebra produce excellent fountain brush pens with cartridge or converter filling systems that allow artists to use any fountain pen ink.

a: Calligraphy inks fall into several categories: India ink (a waterproof, permanent ink made from carbon black and shellac binder, ideal for dip pens but destructive to fountain pens due to the shellac), sumi ink (an East Asian ink made from soot and animal glue, traditionally prepared by grinding an ink stick on an inkstone, producing rich, deep blacks with subtle warm or cool undertones), and calligraphy-specific inks from brands like Pelikan, Higgins, Speedball, and Winsor & Newton that are formulated to flow well through dip nibs without clogging. Fountain pen inks from brands like Diamine, Pilot Iroshizuku, J. Herbin, Noodler's, Colorverse, Rohrer & Klingner, De Atramentis, Sailor, and Platinum offer an enormous range of colors and properties including sheen (metallic highlights where ink pools), shimmer (suspended metallic particles), and shading (color variation within a single stroke from light to dark as the ink pools), with waterproof, archival, pigment-based, and iron gall options available for permanence.

a: Calligraphy and fountain pen paper must be coated or sized to prevent bleed-through, feathering, and ghosting while allowing ink to dry at a reasonable speed and show properties like sheen and shading to their fullest. Tomoe River paper (used in Hobonichi planners and many high-end notebooks) is famously thin yet resists bleed-through, showing sheen and shading better than almost any other paper; Rhodia and Clairefontaine papers have a smooth, coated surface that prevents feathering and makes guidelines easy to follow; and HP Premium 32 laser paper is a budget-friendly favorite for practice, with enough coating to handle many fountain pen and dip pen inks without bleed-through. Practice pads from brands like Canson, Strathmore, and Arches offer hot press (smooth), cold press (textured), and rough surfaces suited to different techniques, while notebook brands like Midori, Life, Apica, Maruman, Leuchtturm, and Nanami Paper cater to calligraphers who write and draw on the go.
